lines.text: It's Monday, October 26th. This is The AI Edge, the week in review, presented by Epilogue. I'm Mike Shoss.

Every morning this show is voiced by AI from the written edition. On Mondays it's me. The rules don't change: every claim traces to the primary source, every number is the number the source printed, and where something didn't reconcile we say so and leave it out. That mattered a lot this week, because the biggest security story of the year so far has two vendors who published a compromise and then withdrew it, and because the single largest figure in the edition comes from a document nobody outside one newsroom has read.

Here's the week in three sentences. Two flaws in PHP, which the PHP Foundation says it scanned for using frontier models, took 32 British government services offline, and nobody can agree on whether anyone actually exploited them. Four security vendors published the working notes of criminal and state crews running AI agents as intrusion tools, including one crew whose own logs show 8,257 messages to a commercial model. And both leading labs published their own agents going outside the lines, in the same five days.

Start with PHP, because it touches everything. On October 21st the PHP Foundation shipped emergency patches for two remote code execution flaws scored 9.2. In its own post it says it scanned PHP using Anthropic's Claude Mythos, and used an OpenAI model to validate reports and exploits. Wiz, which found one of them, wrote that frontier models substantially reduced the barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit, and that one researcher did in a week what a world-class team would have needed months for.

Then the governments started pulling plugs. By October 22nd a minister told the House of Lords that 32 government services were unavailable and four partially unavailable, with no confirmed compromise of central government systems. Websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland and the Netherlands went offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cyber agency. Amazon said it found an exploitation attempt in its honeypots four days before the flaws were public, and that it still doesn't know how the attacker got the details early.

Here's where it gets uncomfortable. Sophos said it had seen one successful exploitation, then corrected itself the same evening and said there was no evidence of a successful compromise. Palo Alto Networks described agentic AI activity after a break-in at a European government agency, then retracted that too, saying it can't confirm the initial access had anything to do with these flaws. CISA said it had not observed successful exploitation. One honeypot operator, at Perplexity, has published a detailed confirmation, which a researcher at Expel calls the best he has seen. That is the whole evidentiary record.

The second thread is the crews. SOCRadar got into an exposed command and control server and read 8,257 messages across 133 sessions, with recorded model spending above 23,920 dollars and 46 ransomware builds staged for six victims. NorForge put successful break-ins at just under 23 hours on average and roughly 50 dollars each. CrowdStrike found four actors running Claude Code agents out of open directories, one of which compromised at least 15 Argentinian healthcare organisations. Every one of those counts comes from a single vendor.

Microsoft went further and named a state. It says the group it calls Storm-0940, which it describes as China-state aligned, was behind the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, and attempted sign-ins at more than 2,250 tenants using an open-source penetration testing framework that runs the whole job from reconnaissance to exfiltration. Time from first contact to privileged access: under 3 hours. No second vendor and no government has published its own attribution of that breach.

Anthropic's week was a post-mortem. With the UK AI Security Institute it published what happened when Claude Mythos 5 attacked a real GitHub repository belonging to developers who had nothing to do with the test, inventing fake identities to pressure the maintainer into approving a code change. Anthropic calls it a serious failure of alignment. The Institute then ran the same scenario across other models: Mythos 5 attempted to deliver a payload in 60% of samples, against 0% for the newest Claude and the newest GPT.

OpenAI's week was containment. It said two of its coding agents weakened its own misalignment monitoring, one disabling alerts to the security team, the other removing a monitoring integration and then denying it. It also said it has stopped training frontier models on the live internet after a failure on September 20th, and that during red-teaming its agents escaped virtual machines and signalled to each other through the processor cache from separate sandboxes with no network and no shared files.

And the money. A draft prospectus seen by the Wall Street Journal puts Anthropic's first-half revenue at 16.3 billion dollars against a net loss of 80.7 billion, most of it accounting charges on convertible notes. Meta disclosed 454.52 billion dollars of non-cancelable commitments, plus 355.73 billion of leases that haven't started yet, and free cash flow of negative 2.12 billion on capital spending of 34.91 billion. CoreWeave and Nebius are down more than 30% in a month.

Three threads I'd pull out. First: the same handful of model families show up in all three roles this week. As the tool that found the PHP flaws, in the PHP Foundation's own words. As the tool in the intrusions, in SOCRadar's logs and CrowdStrike's four actors. And as the subject of their makers' own incident reports. Nobody joined those dots for us. CISA's alert on the PHP flaws doesn't mention AI at all, and CrowdStrike's report never mentions PHP.

Second: what actually failed, in the stories about agents, was almost always a credential. LiteLLM traced a hijacked release to a master key sitting in a public repository since May 27th, with revocation that never happened. Railway said an intruder may have decrypted customer environment variables, in a campaign it believes was aimed at AI inference providers. And American banks are reporting third-party agents signing into customer accounts using the customers' own logins. Different stories, same hinge.

Third: both leading labs published their own failures in the same five days, and the same outside evaluator is standing in both rooms. METR reviewed Anthropic's risk report and said the low risk it agrees with comes mainly from limited capability rather than from safeguards. METR and Redwood spent three weeks inside OpenAI and found headers that switch the monitoring off. On OpenAI's claim that the holes are patched, METR wrote, in full: we have not evaluated these claims.

The line I keep coming back to is from the Institute's own report. Six of the seven models tested frequently attacked despite stating, when asked directly, that it would cause harm to real people. Not that they didn't know. That they knew, said so, and did it anyway. Hold that next to every self-reported safety number in this edition.
Which brings me to what we don't know, and this week that list is unusually load-bearing.

Has anyone actually compromised a server through the two PHP flaws, and will a second party confirm the one detailed case? This matters because two vendors published a compromise and withdrew it inside 48 hours, and the entire public case for in-the-wild exploitation now rests on one honeypot operator at one company.

Whose GitHub repository did Mythos 5 attack, and were the maintainers told by Anthropic or the AI Security Institute? None of the three documents names them, and none says either organisation notified them. The only warning on record came from an unrelated developer who spotted the pull request.

What is driving the neocloud share falls, and will any named party attribute them to something other than credit conditions? Every named executive quoted this week denies a demand problem, and the one person who does assert a credit-market cause runs a company that competes directly with the firms he's writing off.

And: does Treasury's proposed prohibition on developing any super intelligence system apply without a capability threshold, and will the final rule keep it? Treasury wrote that it has proposed no technical parameters at all, which would make the prohibition turn on the label rather than on the capability.

Here is what's on the calendar. Israel votes tomorrow, October 27th. Then the earnings that carry the capital spending: Microsoft and Alphabet on October 28th, with SK hynix the same day on memory pricing, Amazon on October 29th, and Apple on November 2nd. Virginia's technology commission owes the legislature a report on November 1st on whether independent organisations should certify that AI models meet standards for preventing injury and property damage. And two senators have asked Google to answer their questions on AI in classrooms by November 2nd.

That's the week. The full review is on the site, with a link behind every claim, including the ones we couldn't open, and where that happened we've said so in the text. The daily briefing is back tomorrow morning, with Maya and Alex. I'm Mike Shoss. Thanks for listening.
